entry.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

link.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

entry.content:
A language model can produce a loop invariant, a function contract or a patch in seconds. It cannot tell you whether any of those things is actually correct. A model checker can. Unwinding assertions confirm that a loop bound covers every iteration, k-induction proves properties of unbounded executions, and ranking functions prove that loops terminate. The checker still needs a property to verify, and for deep/nested loops and large codebases the proof often depends on an invariant or contract that no one has written. Each side fills a gap in the other.

Since 2023 our Systems and Software Security (S3) group at the University of Manchester and our collaborators have looked at what happens when the two share a loop. Much of this work has used ESBMC, the SMT-based model checker that we develop. ESBMC combines abstract interpretation through interval analysis, model checking through bounded model checking and k-induction, deductive verification through function contracts [1], and SMT solving. A recent survey looks at how it has become the verification backend for LLM-based tools [2].

flowchart LR
    T["Task<br/>program, property,<br/>or requirement"] --> L["LLM proposes<br/>code, patch, invariant,<br/>contract, spec, translation"]
    L --> V{"Formal tool checks<br/>ESBMC,<br/>automated theorem prover"}
    V -- "holds" --> A["Accepted artifact<br/>with a proof or<br/>bounded guarantee"]
    V -- "fails" --> C["Counterexample<br/>trace, line, property"]
    C --> L

Figure 1. The loop shared by most of the papers below. The LLM never makes the correctness decision; the formal tool does.

Our work since 2023

1. How safe is LLM-generated code?

We started off by asking how often LLM-written code is unsafe, and used ESBMC to find out. More than half of the C programs that GPT-3.5-turbo wrote for our FormAI dataset had at least one vulnerability [3], and a follow-up across nine LLMs found at least 62% [4].

Model checking every completion is too slow for an IDE, so we used these verifier-checked labels to train SecureFalcon, a small classifier that flags vulnerable code instantly on a CPU [5].

Formal tools have blind spots too. On the CASTLE benchmark, ESBMC raised the fewest false alarms but missed vulnerabilities outside the properties it checks, such as weak cryptography, while LLMs got worse as programs grew [6]. A survey chapter covers the wider area [7].

2. Counterexample-guided repair and generation

When ESBMC finds a violation, it returns a counterexample: a concrete input and the execution trace that leads to the failing check. That makes it a precise bug report, so we pass it back to an LLM. ESBMC-AI (posted May 2023) takes the source code, the counterexample and the stack trace and feeds it to an LLM, and ESBMC then re-verifies the patch. It was evaluated on 50k FormAI programs [8]. ESBMC-AI has since been succeeded by Entoli, an open-source agent with formal-verification-based workflows. The same loop also works for neural-network code: ESBMC checked about 81k mutated neural-network programs, and an LLM repaired the bugs that ESBMC found [9]. VeriExploit runs it in reverse: you start with a Solidity counterexample and an LLM generates an attacker contract which re-triggers the bug. That contract is then validated by a model checker and is able to reproduce 85.60% of the bugs in our benchmark [10]. For legacy C code, UnitTenX turns ESBMC counterexamples into readable unit tests [11].

3. LLMs supply what the verifier is missing

Here the LLM writes out the invariants and contracts that a proof needs, and a sound tool then decides whether to believe them.

  • Invariants. ESBMC ibmc replaces each loop with an LLM-generated invariant which a theorem prover then checks. It was able to verify programs that SeaHorn and VeriAbs were unable to verify and went on to receive an ACM SIGSOFT Distinguished Paper Award [12]. VerIbmc takes the same approach using open-weight models on a single local machine and solves 431 of the 499 problems in its best configuration, GPT-OSS-120B [13].
  • Contracts. ConVer takes a top-level property and synthesizes function contracts from it, refining them in a CEGAR-CEGIS loop and achieving 82-96% success on 45 Frama-C programs, the easiest of its four benchmark suites, and as low as 33% on the harder ones [14]. For regression verification, partial LLM-inferred contracts produced zero false equivalence proofs on EqBench-C [15].
  • Agents. Agentic model checking is based on the principle of ‘agents propose, solvers verify’ where the agent works out the specifications and plans the run, with all soundness-critical decisions remaining with the bounded model checker (CBMC and Kani). On mature, heavily fuzzed software it found 68 source-audited defects across 11 projects [16].

4. From prose and other languages to checkable models

SpecVerify uses Claude 3.5 Sonnet in conjunction with ESBMC to derive properties from requirements. On nine of Lockheed Martin’s cyber-physical systems it achieved the same result as NASA’s CoCoSim but with fewer false positives [17]. The models still occasionally misread the specifications, so human review remained necessary. INVAR takes a document (e.g. the USB 2.0 or CXL 4.0 specification) and extracts a transition system from it, which it then checks with NuSMV and reports any missing evidence as a named gap rather than a vacuous pass [18]. With NASA JPL we use an LLM to translate Python into C for ESBMC. The paper makes the caveat that as the translation doesn’t prove equivalence the outcome is only bug finding and not verification [19]; the agent and benchmark are both public.

5. Reviews of the field

Two reviews place this work in a wider context: one which provides a taxonomy of the generative transformations and their recurring patterns in over 100 LLM-based proposals for software verification and falsification [20], and one which is a systematic review of 38 studies on LLM agents, which identifies specification as the bottleneck rather than checking [21].

How the pieces fit together

timeline
    2023 : FormAI dataset
         : ESBMC-AI preprint
    2024 : LLM invariants, ESBMC ibmc
         : Repair of neural-network code
    2025 : FormAI-v2, nine LLMs
         : SecureFalcon, CASTLE
         : SpecVerify, VeriExploit, UnitTenX
    2026 : ConVer, VerIbmc, partial contracts
         : Python translation, INVAR
    2027 : Agentic model checking

Figure 2. Timeline by publication year, or by first preprint for ESBMC-AI and for work not yet at a venue.

The papers all follow the same pattern of division of labor. The LLM does the semantic guessing (what a loop maintains, what a function assumes, what a requirement means). A sound tool provides the guarantee. Over time the LLM has been trusted to do more and more. It started off just being measured, then it was used to repair code under a whole-program verifier, then it was used to write parts of the proof and in the agentic model checking work it’s used to plan the entire run. Invariants and contracts are proved before they are used, so a wrong guess is rejected. Assumptions about the environment are different: they are trusted, not checked. If an LLM writes an assumption that rules out every input reaching an assertion, the verifier reports success vacuously. That is why our pipelines check the evidence itself: each LLM-written harness has a seeded-bug twin that must fail, and INVAR reports missing evidence as a gap rather than a pass. A number of the papers are also direct extensions of one another. FormAI provided the evaluation set for ESBMC-AI and the training data for SecureFalcon. VerIbmc builds on the ibmc invariant work.

The negative results are just as important as the positive ones. CASTLE shows us the limitations of the formal tools. SpecVerify shows that the prose still requires a human to read it. The Python work is very clear that, without a verified translation, the method can find bugs but cannot prove the code correct.

Lessons learned

Benchmarks come with an answer key; production code does not. In recent work an LLM agent drafted verification harnesses for codebases such as the AWS SDK for C++, NVIDIA OpenSMA firmware and vLLM, ESBMC checked them, and maintainers merged 18 fixes upstream, including fixes for two CVEs in the AWS SDK for C++. Five lessons from that work and the papers above, presented at FATTW 2026:

  1. Zero false positives beats a higher proof rate. Developers stop trusting a tool that raises false alarms.
  2. Maintainers fix what arrives with a concrete input. The counterexample is the bug report.
  3. The generator’s quality still propagates. With GPT-4o instead of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, SpecVerify produced 8 false positives instead of 0.
  4. We do not win every benchmark. SeaHorn proves more programs than ibmc, and CoCoSim matches SpecVerify; portfolios beat single tools.
  5. Verifiers have traps too. Zero verification conditions, disabled unwinding assertions and contracts that silently check nothing all look like success, so the evidence itself needs checking.

What comes next

The talk closes with three challenges that neither academia nor industry can solve alone:

  • Verification at generation speed. Agents generate code in seconds, while industrial proofs take minutes to hours. Program verification is undecidable in general (Rice’s theorem), so some checks will end in a timeout or an unknown verdict however fast the tools get. Checking must reuse earlier proofs incrementally and report honestly when it cannot decide.
  • Guarantees for agent workflows. Verifying each agent is not enough to verify the workflow they form; we need compositional contracts between agents.
  • Evidence we can trust. DO-178C already accepts formal evidence through DO-333, which raises the question of who checks the checker. Witnesses and validators are part of the answer.

Underneath all three sits the problem that every line of work above runs into: how do we validate a specification an LLM has derived from natural language before anything is proved against it?

Join us

We’re looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators who are interested in working on these problems (formal methods, program analysis, machine learning etc). Our tools are open source and most of the papers listed above come with the associated artifacts so you can run them. If this is of interest to you then just get in touch with Lucas Cordeiro with a brief note on what you’d like to work on. To talk with the group first, join our public Zulip chat.

entry.summary: How our group has combined LLMs with model checking, SMT solving and theorem proving since 2023 and where we think the open problems are.

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. entry.summary: We’re sharing updates across our Gemini family of models and a glimpse of Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants.
